title: Understanding tasklist
description: Displays running processes on local or remote Windows systems, with options to filter, format, and show modules, services, and verbose details.
summary: Displays running processes on local or remote Windows systems, with options to filter, format, and show modules, services, and verbose details.

examples.description: Lists all running processes on the local computer in a table.
Shows verbose details for processes that are not responding.
Lists only processes whose image name matches chrome.exe.
Outputs, in CSV without headers, processes using more than ~500,000 KB of memory.
Shows which services are hosted by each svchost.exe instance.
Lists processes that have loaded ntdll.dll (and shows loaded modules).
Prompts for the password and lists processes on remote host SRV01 using the specified credentials.

important_fields.description: Executable name of the process; use to identify the application (e.g., chrome.exe, svchost.exe).
Unique process identifier; essential for correlating logs and for targeted termination with taskkill.
Approximate working set in KB; high values can indicate memory leaks or runaway processes.
Indicates RUNNING, NOT RESPONDING, or UNKNOWN; helps quickly spot hung apps.
Account under which the process runs; useful for security context and ownership checks.
Cumulative CPU time used; sustained high values can indicate CPU-bound processes.
Lists Windows services hosted in the process; critical for mapping svchost.exe instances to services.
Shows loaded DLLs; useful for dependency and injection analysis.
Terminal Services session information; helps identify interactive vs. service sessions.
Top-level window title for GUI apps; helps match processes to visible windows.

explanation.title: Understanding the command
explanation.purpose: tasklist helps technicians quickly inventory running processes, correlate PIDs, isolate unresponsive apps, and map services and modules for deeper diagnostics.
explanation.when_to_use: Use when you need to identify a process by name or PID, detect hung applications, investigate high memory/CPU usage, determine which services a host process runs, or enumerate processes on a remote machine.

what_to_check.name: High MEMUSAGE values
what_to_check.description: Points to memory-intensive processes; sustained growth suggests a memory leak.

what_to_check.name: High CPUTIME
what_to_check.description: Indicates CPU-bound processes that may affect system responsiveness.

what_to_check.name: STATUS = NOT RESPONDING
what_to_check.description: Flags applications that are hung; consider further triage or termination.

what_to_check.name: svchost.exe with /svc
what_to_check.description: Reveals which Windows services are inside each host process to pinpoint a misbehaving service.

what_to_check.name: MODULES containing suspicious DLLs
what_to_check.description: Helps detect unusual injections or problematic libraries loaded into processes.

interpretation.title: Multiple identical IMAGENAME entries
interpretation.message: The application is multi-process (e.g., browsers) or has spawned workers; look at PID, MEMUSAGE, and CPUTIME to find the heavy instance.

interpretation.title: STATUS shows NOT RESPONDING
interpretation.message: The UI thread is hung; check CPUTIME and MEMUSAGE. If persistent, consider saving data and using taskkill by PID.

interpretation.title: High MEMUSAGE trending upward
interpretation.message: Likely leak in the process; confirm with repeated sampling and consider restarting the service or application.

interpretation.title: svchost.exe consuming resources
interpretation.message: Use tasklist /svc to identify hosted services; then investigate or restart the specific service rather than all svchost instances.

interpretation.title: Remote query fails with RPC/unavailable
interpretation.message: Check target is reachable, credentials are admin on target, RPC (TCP 135 and dynamic ports) allowed through firewall, and remote UAC restrictions.

explanation.common_mistake: Forgetting quotes around the /FI filter value (e.g., using /fi status eq running instead of /fi "status eq running"), causing parsing errors or incorrect results.
explanation.permissions_notes: Local use typically works as a standard user. Remote use (/S) generally requires local administrator rights on the target, proper credentials (/U, /P), network connectivity, and firewall allowance for RPC. UAC remote restrictions may block administrative local accounts unless using the built-in Administrator or appropriate policy settings.
explanation.risk_warning: tasklist is read-only, but frequent remote enumerations can add minor overhead and will create authentication and audit log entries.

explanation.narrative: I start with tasklist to get the running processes. If the system is sluggish, I filter for high MEMUSAGE or NOT RESPONDING to find offenders. When I see a hot svchost.exe, I rerun with /svc to map services. With the PID in hand, I decide whether to stop just the offending service or to terminate the process. If the issue is on a remote host, I use /S with admin credentials and verify RPC/firewall if it fails.
